headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from Cursor↔Flowise shared-file and tool-automation workflows.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads and writes workspace files and clipboard contents, while Flowise reads/writes server filesystem and uploaded files. That creates a plausible shared-content bridge where attacker-controlled text from one can be treated as instructions by the other. The pathway is not provably blocked, but it is not inherently a direct parser hijack in the profiles.
conditions: IF Cursor opens a file or clipboard payload produced by Flowise without provenance checks
IF Flowise ingests files that Cursor previously edited and later reuses them as prompt content
mitigations: Separate workspaces and uploaded-file directories
Disable clipboard-based handoff between the tools
Add a provenance header to shared files
Review any file that contains instructions before reuse
requires-engineering: enforce content-type and trust boundaries in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents; Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and uploaded files. Because both have broad network egress and filesystem access, sensitive material can flow from a shared workspace into either agent’s outbound model/API calls. The profiles do not show a hard isolation boundary, so leakage is plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or upload directory
IF either agent forwards file contents or clipboard contents to a model provider or HTTP tool
mitigations: Use separate directories for code and Flowise uploads
Remove secrets from shared files before opening them
Restrict outbound model providers to approved tenants
Turn off clipboard transfer for sensitive sessions
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before any outbound call

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can modify git state and write the filesystem; Flowise can also write the filesystem and runs with server-side shared state. If both operate on the same directory or repo, concurrent writes can overwrite each other or corrupt git history. The profiles show no locking or coordination primitive, so the conflict is dangerous by default once they share a mutable workspace.
conditions: IF Cursor and Flowise target the same repository or filesystem path
IF either agent writes while the other is editing or committing the same files
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git branches per agent
Check for file locks before writes
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise is an orchestration layer that can turn upstream text into tool-node actions, while Cursor can generate code and commands inside the editor. If Flowise consumes Cursor-produced output without verification, mistakes or hallucinated facts can cascade into automated actions or code changes. The pair lacks a documented verification step in the profiles, so the downstream blast radius is substantial.
conditions: IF Flowise uses Cursor-generated text as an input to tool nodes or HTTP actions
IF Cursor-generated code or instructions are executed without human review
mitigations: Require human approval before Flowise tool execution
Insert a validation step between Cursor and Flowise
Limit Flowise to read-only tools for shared tasks
Review generated code before running it
requires-engineering: add schema validation for all inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor handles clipboard contents and model-provider API keys, while Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and tool credentials. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into the shared workflow, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches across two different vendors. The profiles do not document aligned compliance controls, so the mismatch risk is real but not proven to be a breach by itself.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into Cursor and then propagated into Flowise chatflows
IF one system retains prompts or uploads longer than the other for the same data class
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared prompts
Purge chatflow inputs after use
Review vendor retention settings
Keep secrets out of clipboard and uploads
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies across both vendors
